name: -C target-cpu=native
baseline: cargo build --release for the target's default generic CPU
verdict_reason: It helps code with loops LLVM can vectorize, but it is not a general speedup. When the rust-lang project built rustc for x86-64-v3, the reviewer called the result a significant wall-time loss despite instruction-count gains of up to 2.5-6.6% on a few benchmarks, and native binaries can fail on older CPUs.
tier_reason: A rust-lang project measurement on rustc-perf, though from 2020 (LLVM 11 era) and using x86-64-v3 rather than native; the Rust Performance Book gives no numbers.
claimed_speedup: Rust Performance Book: can improve runtime speed, especially with vectorization opportunities (no numbers). rustc built for x86-64-v3: instruction counts down up to -2.5% (inflate-check) and -6.6% (keccak-debug), but 'a pretty significant wall time loss' overall; x86-64-v2 'a slight win (or perhaps lost in the noise)'
workload: The Rust compiler built with -Ctarget-cpu=x86-64-v2 and x86-64-v3, timed on the rustc-perf suite
toolchain: rustc with a backported LLVM patch adding x86-64-v2/v3/v4 CPU levels (November 2020)
platforms: All targets; 'native' means the build machine's CPU
one_liner: Compiling for the build machine's exact CPU helps vectorizable loops; for general code measured gains were nil or negative.
how_it_is_fast: target-cpu=native lets LLVM use every instruction-set extension on the build machine, such as AVX2 or AVX-512, and tune for that CPU. Loops that auto-vectorize can process more data per instruction; branchy code with little data parallelism changes little.
use_it_when: Binaries built and run on the same machine or a uniform fleet
Numeric or data-parallel loops that LLVM can auto-vectorize
skip_it_when: Distributing binaries: they can fail with illegal-instruction errors on older CPUs
Branchy, pointer-heavy code such as compilers and parsers, where the measured effect was nil or negative
Cross-compiling, where 'native' describes the wrong machine
caveats: The only measured numbers found are from 2020 and target x86-64-v3, not native
The test program was rustc; numeric code may benefit more
tradeoffs: Output depends on the build machine, so builds differ across machines

evidence.quote: This can improve runtime speed, especially if the compiler finds vectorization opportunities in your code.
This PR instructs rustbuild to compile the compiler with the -Ctarget-cpu=x86-64-v2 option enabled in hope of getting some optimization gains from autovectorization.
V3 looks like a pretty significant wall time loss, V2 looks like a slight win (or perhaps lost in the noise). My guess is that this is not worth it at this time.
Yeah there are some single digit improvements in instruction counts (up to -2.5% in inflate-check full for v3, up to -6.6% in keccak-debug full)
